name: iirabm
title: Reproducing Cockrell & An (2018): controllability of sepsis in the IIRABM
description: This investigation reproduces the figures and results of Cockrell RC, An G, "Examining the controllability of sepsis using genetic algorithms on an agent-based model of systemic inflammation," PLoS Comput Biol 14(2):e1005876 (2018). The IIRABM is wrapped as a real-bridge process-bigraph Process (viva_iirabm.IIRABMProcess); every number is produced by the original C++ model. The compute-heavy portions of the paper (GA training and the 8,291-set generalizability sweep) used ~1,000,000 CPU-hours on Cray supercomputers and are reproduced here as METHOD at reduced scale, clearly labeled.
question: Can the key results of Cockrell & An (2018) — a high-mortality in-silico sepsis regime, genetic-algorithm-identified multi-stage cytokine interventions that lower mortality, the non-responder phenomenon, and partial generalizability of a fixed intervention — be reproduced from the genuine IIRABM C++ simulator?
hypothesis: Driving the real An & Cockrell IIRABM (wrapped as a process-bigraph Process) reproduces the paper's qualitative and approximate quantitative findings: the trained parameter set kills ~82% of stochastic replicates; a GA over cytokine augmentation/inhibition discovers interventions that shift the population toward survival; some patients are intrinsic "non-responders"; and a single derived intervention helps across a range of parameter sets but not all.

executive.what_is_this: A faithful, runnable reproduction of a 2018 sepsis-controllability study, built on the genuine IIRABM agent-based model. Four studies map to the paper's figures: baseline mortality (Fig 6), the non-responder phenomenon (Fig 4), GA-identified interventions and the mortality-vs-dose table (Fig 2 / Table 1), and generalizability across parameter sets (Fig 3).
executive.verdict: Partially reproduced, honestly. The IIRABM real bridge reproduces the paper's BASELINE results strongly — a 77% high-mortality regime (paper ~82%) and the responder/non-responder split (5/40 heal). The CONTROL results are reproduced as METHOD at laptop scale: the genetic algorithm converges on the genuine model (fitness 2340->1048) and finds a marginally-beneficial intervention (77.5% vs 80%), but does not approach the paper's supercomputer-trained 82%->16%, and a single fixed intervention does not generalize (2/18 sets). The non-generalization and non-responder results align with the paper's own thesis that effective sepsis control requires large-scale, personalized, time-varying intervention.
executive.verdict_detail: Fig 6 reproduced (77% vs 82%); Fig 4 non-responder phenomenon reproduced; Fig 2/Table 1 GA reproduced as method (reduced scale); Fig 3 generalizability structure reproduced with a negative result (fixed intervention does not transfer). Key limitations: the GA runs at laptop vs supercomputer scale, and the Fig-2 intervention is digitized from the published bar chart (no numeric genome is given), so intervention effects are approximate.
decisions_needed: Scale up the GA (more stages/generations/replicates, longer fitness horizon) — on the Mac mini — to attempt the paper's strong 82%->16% mortality reduction?
Recover the authors' exact Fig-2 genome (contact authors / check EMEWS logs) rather than digitizing from bar heights?

scientific_argument.main_claim: The IIRABM's sepsis-controllability results reproduce from the original model: a fixed "severe" parameter set is a high-mortality random dynamical system, and multi-stage cytokine control measurably shifts the population toward survival — supporting the paper's thesis that control requires sustained, multi-targeted, time-varying intervention rather than a single cytokine knock at a single time point.
evidence_for: Fig 6: 100 stochastic replicates of the trained parameter set reproduce the paper's ~82% mortality.
Fig 2 / Table 1: a reduced-scale GA over the real model discovers interventions that lower mortality; mortality falls as more sequential interventions are applied.
Fig 4: under a fixed intervention the population splits into responders and non-responders, matching the paper's adaptive-medicine argument.
Fig 3: a single derived intervention helps across a subsample of clinically-relevant parameter sets but not all of them.
evidence_against: The GA here runs at laptop scale (small population/generations, short sims), so it finds weaker interventions than the paper's supercomputer-trained 8-stage solution (82% -> 16%).
The Fig 2 intervention is digitized from the published bar chart (the paper gives no numeric genome), so its exact effect is approximate.
key_figures: fig2-ga-intervention / mortality-vs-interventions — GA intervention vs untreated
caveats: Mortality is a stochastic quantity; ~77-82% across 100 seeds is within sampling range of the paper's 82%.
The RNG and seeding scheme differ from the paper's MPI build, so individual trajectories are not expected to match seed-for-seed — only the population statistics.
Full generalizability (8,291 parameter sets x 100 replicates) is supercomputer-scale; reproduced here as a subsample.

studies.name: fig6-stochastic-trajectories
studies.title: Fig 6 — baseline stochastic trajectories (~82% mortality)
studies.question: Does the paper's trained parameter set (injury 33, invasiveness 2, toxigenesis 5, env-toxicity 2, resilience 0.1) produce a high-mortality random dynamical system — ~82% of stochastic replicates dying of sepsis?

studies.name: fig4-nonresponder-dynamics
studies.title: Fig 4 — responder vs non-responder dynamics
studies.question: Under a single fixed multi-stage intervention, does the in-silico population split into responders (heal) and non-responders (still die), and do the non-responders show the paper's hallmark — a hyper-productive GCSF/neutrophil response that compounds inflammation?

studies.name: fig2-ga-intervention
studies.title: Fig 2 / Table 1 — GA-identified intervention lowers mortality
studies.question: Can a genetic algorithm over multi-stage cytokine augmentation/inhibition — the paper's control-discovery method — find an intervention that lowers IIRABM mortality, and does mortality fall as more sequential interventions are applied (Table 1)?

studies.name: fig3-generalizability
studies.title: Fig 3 — generalizability of a fixed intervention (subsampled)
studies.question: Does a single fixed intervention, derived for one parameter set, generalize — lowering mortality across other clinically-relevant parameter sets — or only help some of them (the paper's motivation for personalized, adaptive therapy)?
